name: The Last Supper
kicker: Leonardo’s mural of Jesus’s final meal · A landmark of linear perspective
briefing: In a Milan monastery’s dining hall, Leonardo da Vinci painted thirteen men sharing a meal, freezing the exact moment Jesus announces that one of them will betray him. Leonardo used a risky paint recipe instead of true fresco, so the mural began flaking within his own lifetime. It still survived a doorway cut through its bottom edge, soldiers stabling horses in the room, and a World War II bombing raid that wrecked the room around it.

qb.tip: All 8 real tossups lead with the Santa Maria delle Grazie setting, the knocked-over salt cellar, and a bag of silver; several compare Leonardo’s version to Last Supper paintings by Tintoretto and Veronese, who are NOT the answer here.

sample.note: the 8 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: This work’s apostles sit in four groups of three, each group reacting differently to a sudden announcement. Three windows behind the central figure’s head align with the room’s real architecture so every perspective line in the room meets at his right temple.
tossups.r: A doorway cut into the wall in 1652 later sliced off the painted feet of the central figure. For 10 points, name this mural by Leonardo da Vinci showing Jesus and his Twelve Apostles.

tossups.p: Thomas raises his index finger beside the central figure in this work, a gesture some read as foreshadowing his later doubt. A disembodied hand, believed to belong to Peter, holds a knife pointed away from the table.
tossups.r: The betrayer among the diners sits in shadow clutching a bag of silver coins near a knocked-over salt cellar. For 10 points, name this painting of Jesus’s final meal, found in a Milan monastery.

tossups.p: French revolutionary troops stabled horses in the room containing this work in 1796 and scratched at the painted eyes of its figures. A flood around 1800 left roughly two feet of water in that same room, according to the writer Goethe [“GUR-tuh”].
tossups.r: A pupil named Giampietrino [“jahm-pyeh-TREE-no”] painted a nearly full-size copy that later guided restorers. For 10 points, name this mural depicting Jesus’s last meal with his disciples, painted by Leonardo da Vinci.

tossups.p: An 1821 restoration attempt by Stefano Barezzi [“bah-RETZ-ee”], who tried to peel the plaster off in sections, damaged this work further. It faces a Crucifixion fresco by Giovanni Donato da Montorfano [“mohn-tor-FAH-no”] on the opposite wall of the same room.
tossups.r: Sandbags protected it when Allied bombing destroyed the room’s roof in 1943. For 10 points, name this painting of the Twelve Apostles’ final meal with Jesus, located in Milan’s Santa Maria delle Grazie.

tossups.p: Three lunette arches above this work display the coat of arms of the Sforza [“SFORT-sah”] family, who ruled Milan when it was painted. On the far right, the apostles Matthew, Jude Thaddeus, and Simon the Zealot lean together, gesturing back toward the center.
tossups.r: It was painted in tempera on dry plaster rather than true fresco, which caused the paint to begin flaking within years. For 10 points, name this mural of Jesus’s final meal, by Leonardo da Vinci.

tossups.p: In this work, the youthful, androgynous-looking apostle seated to the central figure’s right has sometimes been mistaken by modern novelists for Mary Magdalene, though art historians agree the figure is John. John and Peter lean toward each other in surprise while the betrayer, seated in their same group, leans away.
tossups.r: A copy by one of the artist’s pupils later helped guide its twentieth-century restoration. For 10 points, name this painting showing Jesus’s last meal with his Twelve Apostles.

tossups.p: This work is sometimes contrasted with a version of the same Biblical scene by Paolo Veronese [“veh-roh-NEH-zeh”], which was renamed to refer to the House of Levi after Church officials accused Veronese of indecorum. The painter Tintoretto [“tin-toh-RET-toh”] later depicted the same scene from a dramatic diagonal angle.
tossups.r: Unlike those two versions, this one was painted directly onto a monastery dining-hall wall in Milan. For 10 points, name this depiction of Jesus’s final meal with his apostles, by Leonardo da Vinci.

tossups.p: A twenty-one-year restoration of this work, completed in 1999 and led by Pinin Brambilla Barcilon [“bar-chee-LOHN”], sparked controversy among art historians over how dramatically its colors changed. The mural covers an entire end wall roughly fifteen feet tall and almost twenty-nine feet wide.
tossups.r: Visitors today must reserve tickets and are given only fifteen minutes inside the climate-controlled room to view it. For 10 points, name this Leonardo da Vinci mural of the Twelve Apostles’ final meal with Jesus.

tossups.p: This work was commissioned by Ludovico Sforza, the Duke of Milan, as part of renovations to a Dominican monastery. In it, one apostle tips over a salt cellar, a detail many read as foreshadowing betrayal.
tossups.r: That apostle, Judas, sits in shadow clutching a small bag of silver coins. For 10 points, name this mural depicting the moment Jesus announces that one of his Twelve Apostles will betray him.

tossups.p: In this painting, every orthogonal line of the ceiling and side walls converges on a single point at the central figure’s temple, a triumph of linear perspective. The room it occupies also contains a Crucifixion scene by Montorfano on the facing wall.
tossups.r: A doorway later carved through its base removed the central figure’s painted feet. For 10 points, name this mural of Jesus’s last meal with his twelve disciples, found in Milan, Italy.

tossups.p: This work’s original plaster surface began flaking apart within years, since its creator rejected true fresco for a tempera recipe that let him revise his work slowly. By 1556, the writer Giorgio Vasari already described it as a faded “muddle of blots.”
tossups.r: Despite the damage, its composition of thirteen men around a table remains instantly recognizable. For 10 points, name this painting of Jesus’s final meal, by Leonardo da Vinci.

tossups.p: A copy of this work by the painter Giampietrino, now in London, preserved details that had worn away from the original by the twentieth century. Three windows glow behind the central figure, softly framing his head like a halo.
tossups.r: It depicts thirteen men seated behind a long table on the day before a crucifixion. For 10 points, name this mural of Jesus and his Twelve Apostles sharing a final meal, painted on a Milan monastery wall.

tossups.p: Rather than painting on wet plaster, this work’s creator used a mixture including tempera and oil on dry plaster, trading durability for the ability to work slowly and add fine detail. Three coats of arms belonging to the ruling Sforza family top this work, while a doorway later cut away part of its lower edge.
tossups.r: It depicts the dramatic moment after Jesus tells his disciples that one of them will betray him. For 10 points, name this Leonardo da Vinci mural of the Twelve Apostles’ final meal.

tossups.p: This work’s central figure spreads his hands calmly over the table while the twelve men flanking him erupt into shock, anger, and confusion at his words. One figure beside him raises an index finger, while another, in shadow just left of center, clutches a small bag and leans away into darkness.
tossups.r: Milan’s Santa Maria delle Grazie has housed this mural since the 1490s. For 10 points, name this depiction of Jesus’s last meal with his disciples, painted by Leonardo da Vinci.

tossups.p: Painted for a Dominican monastery’s dining hall, this work shows twelve apostles divided into four groups of three around a central figure, all on one side of a long table. A hidden hand near one edge of the table holds a knife, pointed away from the group, said to belong to the apostle Peter.
tossups.r: Napoleonic troops later used the room housing it as a stable and threw stones at its painted faces. For 10 points, name this Leonardo da Vinci mural depicting Jesus’s final meal with his Twelve Apostles.

clues.t: Painted by the Italian Renaissance master Leonardo da Vinci

Often used as a symbol of the Christian sacrament of Communion (the Eucharist), which traces back to this very meal
Painted on a wall of the refectory (dining hall) of the Santa Maria delle Grazie monastery in Milan, Italy
Commissioned by Ludovico Sforza, the Duke of Milan, as part of renovations to the monastery
Painted in tempera on dry plaster rather than true fresco, which made the paint begin flaking within years

Judas sits in shadow clutching a small bag of silver coins, his payment for the betrayal
A disembodied hand, believed to be Peter’s, holds a knife pointed away from the table
The youthful, androgynous-looking Apostle John sits at Jesus’s right, a figure later misidentified by some novelists as Mary Magdalene
A doorway cut into the wall in 1652 sliced off Jesus’s painted feet

The Twelve Apostles sit in four groups of three, each group reacting differently to the announcement
Three windows behind Jesus’s head align with the room’s real architecture, so every perspective line meets at his right temple
Thomas raises his index finger beside Jesus, a gesture some read as foreshadowing his later doubt
Three lunette arches above the painting display the coat of arms of the ruling Sforza family
A nearly full-size copy by Leonardo’s pupil Giampietrino, now in London, helped guide the painting’s modern restoration

The room flooded with about two feet of water around 1800, according to the writer Goethe
An 1821 restoration attempt by Stefano Barezzi, who tried to peel off and transfer sections of plaster, caused further damage

trap.title: Leonardo’s version, or someone else’s?
trap.body: Many real tossups describe several different paintings of the same Biblical scene in the same breath — Tintoretto’s diagonal table, Paolo Veronese’s version (renamed _The Feast in the House of Levi_ after he was accused of indecorum), and others. All of those are red herrings for a tossup on this answer line.
trap.fix: Listen for the specific setting and details that only belong to Leonardo’s version: the refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, the knocked-over salt cellar, the bag of silver, and the tempera-on-dry-plaster technique that made it flake. If the clue names a different painter as the one who MADE the work being asked about, it is not this answer.
trap.line: Real answer line: The Last Supper (accept Il Cenacolo or L’Ultima Cena).
